title: The solver contract
goal: Six guarantees that hold however the solver reads a miss: a defined entry wins, the solver only fills misses, exact means exact, same strokes same text, a visible mark, one undo; and what is not guaranteed.

blocks.x: [The solver](#/ref/fallback) reads a stroke or `+` run the dictionary lacks. Its reading of a miss is best-effort and changes as it is tuned; these six guarantees do not. Each is a test that builds the whole dictionary as `build` does, packs the solver, and runs real strokes through both in keymux's lookup order (`src/rules/solve/contract_tests.rs`). A broken guarantee fails the build and names itself.

head: Guarantee
In one line
rows: A stroke or run with a dictionary entry types that entry's text. The solver is never asked.
The solver reads only what has no entry
It is a fallback for one-word misses: a single stroke, or a `+` run that is no entry, including a run that is partly entries.
Starred suffix chords, fingerspelled letters, literals, controls and punctuation are fixed points. A longer run is solved around them, never through them.
The same strokes, after the same text, always type the same text.
What the solver read is marked on keymux's tape.
A solver reading is taken back by undo, as any word is.

items: keymux asks each file in its priority order: `01-lyk-commands`, the `02-lyk-` files (alternates, extras, phrases, short, suffixes, words), `03-` names and punctuation, `04-` modifiers. The first file that holds the outline answers; the solver (`05-lyk-solver`) is last.
One outline has one definition: no outline is defined with two different texts across the deployed files.
The backups (`out/lyk/02-lyk-backups.json`) are not deployed, so they are not entries: the solver reads them (guarantee 2).

No entry continues with a starred suffix chord: no deployed outline has one of the 41 starred chords (`+*G`, `+*Z`, `+*EUZ/+-PL`, ...) after its first stroke, except a chord's own entry. The generator gives a word that would use one its next outline, or none (a test builds the dictionary and checks every deployed outline). So a starred chord after a known outline always types that outline's text and the ending, never another word's.
Were the solver asked about a word entry's own outline, it would type that word (entries with a lone `+*` in them excepted: there the solver reads that stroke as the late star).

blocks.x: 2. The solver reads only what has no entry

items: keymux asks a plugin only about one word: a single stroke, or a run whose every stroke after the first carries the join key `+`. Strokes with no `+` between them are separate words and are never one question: `KAT TKOG` is two entries.

A run that is no entry is the solver's, whole, even where its first strokes are entries: it reads known outlines as pieces and the rest by sounds ([how it reads a run](#/ref/fallback/how-it-reads-a-run)).
A run that is an entry stays that entry however it was reached: the strokes before it asked the solver, the last stroke finds the entry.

head: Fixed point
What it is
In a stream or run
rows: An entry defined as an exact attach: `{^}ing`. Its text is glued on as written, with no spelling at the seam.
Inside a run it is never read as sounds, merged or dropped: `TAOEUP/+*G` is *typeing*; `TEF/+*D/+-L` keeps *ed* literal.
A known outline then starred chords
The outline's entry text, then the endings.
`A*R/+*LT` is *arr* + *let*, never *are* + *let*. A plain chord after a starred one is spelled at its seam.
A letter chord with `*` (`A*`, `PW*P`): its own stroke, no `+`.
It ends the run before it and starts nothing: `KAT/+*G A*` is *cating*, then *a*.
The same: each is its own window, typed as its entry.

blocks.x: Verified readings of the solver, each a run with no entry:

head: Strokes
Types
Why
rows: no doubled *n*, and not the near-sounding *raining*
two starred chords in a row
a starred chord, then a plain one
the lock keeps *cat*; the chord adds *ing*
*arr* is the entry, not the commoner *are*

items: The same strokes after the same text type the same text. Nothing else enters: no clock, no earlier strokes beyond the run, no thread, no hash order. Reading a run after any of its prefixes, in any order, on any thread, from fresh or used working memory gives one answer.

**The one dependence on earlier text** is [the word before the run](#/ref/fallback/the-word-before-the-run): it breaks a tie between readings of one kind (homophones). It never moves an entry, a whole known outline, a known outline with starred chords or the text a lock kept, and never turns one kind of reading into another. A *known outline* here is the solver's: an entry of the words, short, alternates or extras files, or one the rules teach ([pieces](#/ref/fallback/3-pieces)); a phrase's, a name's or a command's outline is not one, so a run that starts with one is read from sounds: `UP` is the phrase *you up*, and `UP/+*L` is *app* + *ly* or *up* + *ly*, a tie at one cost, *apply* alone (the commoner word) and *uply* after *the*. With no text before the run there is no dependence.

**Ties have one order.** Readings rank: a whole known outline (or one with starred chords); a known word plus endings that spell a real word; lowest cost (the word before adjusts it); the commoner word; then the order the reading was found in, which is a fixed search order. Equal-cost candidates of a beam keep that order (a stable sort).
The solver's reading code holds no hash map. The packed blob is built the same, byte for byte, whatever order its stems come in.

A stroke whose text the solver read is marked in keymux's tape file: the line ends `plugin:05-lyk-solver "reading"`, after the description. Every stroke of a run carries it, each reading replacing the last. A stroke typed from an entry has no mark.
A reading that comes after keymux's plugin deadline (`plugin_deadline_ms`) types the stroke plain, then arrives as a `late` line with the same mark.

The tape file is the only place: the overlay shows no mark for a solver reading (it shows only the late replacement line). Count the solver's words with `grep -c 'plugin:05-lyk-solver'` on the tape; `lyk mistakes` strips the mark when it reads it.
`*` takes back the last stroke ([punctuation and commands](#/ref/punctuation)). A solver reading of a single stroke is gone after one `*`.
A run of N strokes is read again after each stroke, and each reading replaces the one before. `*` takes back the last stroke and puts back the reading of the first N-1: it takes N `*` to clear a run.
[[TK*UP]] (`{:undo_word}`) takes back the whole word in one stroke, a solver-read run or an entry alike; [[R*EUD]] puts it back whole.

**Which word a miss reads as.** It is the cheapest reading by sounds, rarity and, for a tie, the word before. Rare words, near sounds and homophones can read as another word, and a reading can change when the lexicon or the costs are retuned. `lyk solve --eval 250` measures how often a backup reads as its own word.
**A backup reads as its own word.** Backups are not entries; the solver reads them like any miss.
**A run reads the same midway as at its end.** Each stroke asks again: `KOPL/+PU` reads *champa* and `KOPL/+PU/+TER` reads *computer*.
**The same strokes after different text.** Only a tie between homophones may differ (guarantee 4).
